description: One Solresol word each week, written as notes, digits, colours, and a small playable tune from François Sudre's musical language.

entries.pronunciation: SOL-re-SOL · three spoken or sung notes · 5–2–5
entries.lede: The language names language itself with a tiny arch of three notes: sol, down to re, and home to sol.

origin.note: Sudre's dictionary assigns sol–re–sol to language, idiom, dialect, linguistics, and philology. It also became the conventional name of his system.

sentence.note: A beginner teaching sentence assembled from the dictionary forms dore, domilado, and solresol. Solresol verbs do not inflect for person here.

entries.source_note: The headword and gloss follow the community English dictionary translated from Sudre's original definitions; the sentence is a transparent teaching example, not a quotation from Sudre.

sources.title: Gajewski's Grammar of Solresol, English translation

entries.pronunciation: DO · one spoken or sung note · 1
entries.lede: The first note is Solresol's compact refusal and its ordinary negator: one do can say no or make the next idea negative.

origin.note: The first one-note word is do, meaning no, not, or nor. In a negative clause it stands before the word it negates.

sentence.note: Gajewski's grammar gives this negation pattern in abbreviated note spelling; the full syllable names are expanded here.

entries.source_note: Both the one-note gloss and the position of the negator are explicit in the historical grammar.

entries.pronunciation: RE · one spoken or sung note · 2
entries.lede: Re is the conjunction that lets two things share a phrase without making either one learn harmony.

origin.note: The second one-note word is the coordinating conjunction and.

sentence.note: This deliberately tiny teaching phrase isolates re. Longer examples in the grammar coordinate full noun phrases in the same way.

entries.source_note: The dictionary gives re as and; the teaching phrase keeps the surrounding vocabulary to two basic pronouns.

sources.title: Gajewski's Grammar of Solresol, English translation

entries.pronunciation: MI · one spoken or sung note · 3
entries.lede: Mi is choice compressed to a single note: this or that, cadence optional.

origin.note: The third one-note word is the conjunction or.

sentence.note: A teaching question made entirely from one-note words.

entries.source_note: The glosses of mi, si, and do are all listed in Sudre's one-note vocabulary.

entries.pronunciation: FA · one spoken or sung note · 4
entries.lede: Fa points toward a place or recipient, doing prepositional work with a single green note.

origin.note: The fourth one-note word is a compact preposition translated as at or to.

sentence.note: This is a teaching prepositional phrase rather than a complete clause, kept short so fa's role remains visible.

entries.source_note: The source dictionary gives a broad at/to gloss; English chooses between them from context.

entries.pronunciation: SOL · one spoken or sung note · 5
entries.lede: Sol opens a condition and then waits—musically and grammatically—for the consequence.

origin.note: The fifth one-note word introduces a condition: if.

sentence.note: A deliberately unfinished teaching fragment: a conditional needs something to happen next, and the ellipsis admits it.

entries.source_note: The entry demonstrates the historical one-note gloss without inventing a longer conditional whose tense or word order would distract from it.

entries.pronunciation: LA · one spoken or sung note · 6
entries.lede: La is the definite article—the unusually international-looking member of a vocabulary that otherwise refuses donor-language clues.

origin.note: The sixth one-note word is the definite article the. Its familiar appearance is a consequence of the note name, not an etymological borrowing claim.

sentence.note: A teaching noun phrase using doremi, the dictionary word for day.

entries.source_note: Solresol is a priori: resemblance between la and articles in Romance languages is not treated here as a donor relationship.

entries.pronunciation: SI · one spoken or sung note · 7
entries.lede: At the top of the seven-note ladder, si is assent: yes, agreed, willingly.

origin.note: The seventh one-note word answers yes and can also carry the sense willingly or agreed.

sentence.note: A complete one-word utterance. English-language solfège often calls the seventh note ti; historical Solresol uses si.

entries.source_note: The historical grammar and Sudre-derived dictionary use si, not the later English solfège label ti.

sources.title: Gajewski's Grammar of Solresol, English translation

entries.pronunciation: DO-re · two spoken or sung notes · 1–2
entries.lede: Dore is first person without a compulsory headcount: context and number marking decide whether it is I, me, or we.

origin.note: The binary sequence do–re is the first-person pronoun, covering subject and object uses and, in the dictionary's broad gloss, singular or plural reference.

sentence.note: This is the grammar's basic verb example, expanded from its abbreviated d-r / s-d-f note spelling.

entries.source_note: Gajewski explicitly uses this pattern to show that Solresol verbs keep one form rather than agreeing with the subject.

entries.pronunciation: DO-mi · two spoken or sung notes · 1–3
entries.lede: Domi addresses you without forcing Solresol to ask whether that means one listener or a roomful.

origin.note: The binary sequence do–mi is the second-person pronoun, usable for singular or plural you and in reflexive constructions.

sentence.note: Adapted only by expanding the note names from Gajewski's reflexive-verb example; the repeated pronoun supplies the reflexive object.

entries.source_note: The grammar supplies the construction and the dictionary supplies the broad second-person gloss.

entries.pronunciation: DO-fa · two spoken or sung notes · 1–4
entries.lede: Dofa handles the rest of the pronoun crowd: people, things, singulars, and plurals, with context and prosody doing the sorting.

origin.note: The binary sequence do–fa is the third-person pronoun across subject and object uses. Historical descriptions separately mark gender and number when needed.

sentence.note: A teaching adaptation of the grammar's dore sidofa verb example, substituting the documented third-person pronoun.

entries.source_note: The English dictionary deliberately lists several third-person English pronouns because Solresol does not divide this basic form the same way.

sources.title: Gajewski's Grammar of Solresol, English translation

entries.pronunciation: MI-do · two spoken or sung notes · 3–1
entries.lede: Mido turns toward purpose or beneficiary; reversing its notes to domi produces you, which is peak Rootle mischief.

origin.note: The binary sequence mi–do is translated as for and can introduce purpose. Reversal matters in Solresol: do–mi is the second-person pronoun instead.

sentence.note: A minimal teaching phrase. The historical dictionary's gloss is broader than this single English use.

entries.source_note: The reversal comparison is a structural observation from the two independently listed dictionary forms, not a claim that one was historically derived from the other.

sources.title: Gajewski's Grammar: opposite words by reversal

entries.lede: Doredo returns to its opening note. Its assigned meaning is time.

sentence.note: A newly assembled teaching phrase: la plus doredo. It makes no claim to be a historical quotation.

entries.source_note: The sequence comes from Gajewski’s time vocabulary group. Digits and colours encode those same notes; they add no new words.

sources.title: Gajewski: Grammar of Solresol, English translation

entries.lede: The next do–sol–do is a vocabulary item, not a request to sing for supper.

origin.note: Gajewski gives dosoldo (dsod) as be hungry.

sentence.note: A newly assembled teaching sentence using the listed pronoun and predicate. Pause between its two words.

entries.source_note: In the abbreviated source form dsod, so means sol and d means do. The English are belongs to the translation.

sources.title: Gajewski: Grammar of Solresol, English translation

entries.lede: Three rising notes give the learner something to say after a question.

origin.note: Gajewski lists refasi (rfs) for answering or replying.

sentence.note: A newly assembled teaching sentence. The verb uses the unmarked form shown in the grammar.

entries.source_note: The headword appears in Gajewski’s discussion of grouping synonyms. Its definition is assigned vocabulary, not an etymology from note names.

sources.title: Gajewski: Grammar of Solresol, English translation

entries.lede: Two notes can approve the food. Gajewski uses fala when explaining how to make good into very good.

origin.note: Gajewski lists fala, abbreviated fl, with good and tasty senses. Its note sequence is assigned vocabulary, not a borrowing.

sentence.note: Gajewski gives this phrase as fs fl in the Fasi Sifa section. Here the abbreviated note names are expanded to full syllables; this is a historical example, not a newly attributed quotation.

entries.source_note: The grammar places fasi before an adjective to intensify it. The digits and colours encode the same fa–la sequence; the site’s C-major pitches are a playback choice.

sources.title: Gajewski: Grammar of Solresol, two-syllable vocabulary and Fasi Sifa

entries.lede: Do–si–do offers help. The grammar gathers several English near-synonyms under this one assigned sequence.

origin.note: Gajewski explicitly gives dosido, abbreviated dsd, for helping or assisting in his discussion of synonyms.

sentence.note: A newly assembled teaching sentence using the documented pronouns dore and domi. The present verb is unmarked, and the three words should be separated by pauses.

entries.source_note: The source prints both the full word dosido and the shortened dsd, fixing the middle note as si. The teaching sentence is editorial; the historical assignment of the headword is Gajewski’s.

sources.title: Gajewski: Grammar of Solresol, Suppression of Synonyms and pronouns

entries.lede: A small thank-you needs only two notes. Reading the abbreviation correctly is the larger task.

origin.note: Gajewski’s two-syllable list gives sos for thanking or thanks. His abbreviation so means sol, while s means si.

sentence.note: A teaching utterance newly punctuated from the documented vocabulary item. It is not presented as a sentence quoted from the grammar.

entries.source_note: Parse the source’s sos as so + s: sol followed by si. The colour and digit versions are alternate spellings of those notes, not related words with separate etymologies.

sources.title: Gajewski: Grammar of Solresol, two-syllable words and shortened initials
